title: 6.2 — Gauss–Markov, BLUE and Estimability
breadcrumb: Unit VI → Regression and linear models → 6.2 Gauss–Markov, BLUE and estimability
engineName: Move from the linear model to unbiased estimators, least squares and estimable functions.

sheet: Gauss–Markov: E(u|X)=0 and V(u|X)=σ²I, with X full column rank for the standard inverse form.
BLUE: OLS has minimum variance among linear unbiased estimators.
Normality is not required for BLUE.
a′β is estimable iff a lies in row(X), equivalently C(X′).
Full column rank makes every linear combination of β estimable.
If X′X is singular, use rank/estimability reasoning; do not apply an ordinary inverse.
cards: All components and linear combinations are estimable.
tricks: Write X explicitly from the observation equations before multiplying.
Check X′X diagonal entries by column sums of squares and off-diagonal entries by cross-products.
Verify the proposed estimator by checking its expectation and coefficient weights.
For estimability, solve X′c=a or test a against row(X).
shortcuts: If X′X is diagonal, invert each diagonal element separately.
A′β is estimable exactly when a is a linear combination of the rows of X.
For a full-column-rank design, every linear function of β is estimable.
remember: BLUE is a comparison class: linear and unbiased estimators.
Equal error variances alone do not imply uncorrelated errors; σ²I is the spherical covariance assumption used here.

scenes.title: Refresh the matrix tools
scenes.objective: Rebuild the three prerequisites used in linear estimation.
body: This lesson turns a regression model into an estimator. The algebra uses matrix products, expectations and rank. If one of these tools feels rusty, rebuild it here before moving on.
The aim is not to memorise a formula. It is to understand where each part of the OLS estimator comes from and how to check whether a parameter function can be estimated.

refresh: Transpose means exchange rows and columns. The first row of A becomes the first column of A′.
The second row becomes the second column. Thus [[1,2],[3,4]]′=[[1,3],[2,4]].
In regression, X′ turns the design matrix's columns into rows so X′X and X′y can be formed.

items.ask: If E(X)=μ and a,b are constants, what is E(aX+b)?
refresh: Expectation is the probability-weighted average of a random quantity. For a discrete variable taking values 0 and 4 with equal probabilities, E(X)=0(1/2)+4(1/2)=2. The average is not required to be one of the values the variable can actually take.
Linearity means constants can be pulled outside expectation and sums can be separated: E(aX+b)=aE(X)+b. Here a and b are fixed numbers, so E(b)=b. For example, if E(X)=3, then E(2X+5)=2(3)+5=11.
In the OLS proof, the estimator is β̂=β+(X′X)⁻¹X′u. Taking conditional expectation gives β+(X′X)⁻¹X′E(u|X). The zero conditional mean assumption sets the final term to zero, leaving β.

items.ask: What does full column rank mean for an n×k matrix X?
items.recall: Its k columns are linearly independent; rank(X)=k.
refresh: Column rank counts the number of independent columns.
Full column rank k means no column is an exact linear combination of the others.
Then X′X is invertible, allowing the ordinary OLS formula (X′X)⁻¹X′y.

scenes.title: What does BLUE actually promise?
scenes.objective: Interpret the comparison behind the Gauss–Markov theorem.
body: Suppose several methods estimate the same regression coefficient. Some are biased. Some are nonlinear. Some are linear and unbiased but have different variances.

The Gauss–Markov theorem says that, under its assumptions, ordinary least squares has the smallest variance among all linear unbiased estimators. That is the meaning of BLUE: Best Linear Unbiased Estimator.
The word best is restricted to this comparison class. It does not say OLS is best among every imaginable estimator, and it does not require normally distributed errors.

scenario.teaser: A policy team estimates a wage-return coefficient
scenario.title: Why the comparison class matters
body: A policy team uses a linear regression to estimate the association between years of training and wages. The design matrix records the intercept and training variable for each sampled worker.
The team wants an estimator that is unbiased and linear in the observed outcomes. Many weighted combinations of the outcomes may be unbiased, but their variances need not be equal.

Under the Gauss–Markov assumptions, OLS is the minimum-variance choice within that class. If the team wants likelihood-based efficiency among nonlinear estimators, or exact small-sample distributional statements, additional assumptions and theory are needed.
This is why BLUE is a precise theorem statement, not a general claim that OLS is universally optimal.
scenario.q: What is the comparison class in BLUE?
scenario.answer: All linear unbiased estimators of the regression parameter.

ask.q: Does BLUE require normally distributed errors?
ask.nudge: Separate the first two moments used by Gauss–Markov from assumptions used for exact t and F distributions.

scenes.title: The geometry of least squares
scenes.objective: See OLS as a projection and connect it to the normal equations.
body: OLS chooses β̂ so that the fitted vector Xβ̂ is as close as possible to y in squared Euclidean distance. The residual e=y−Xβ̂ is orthogonal to every column of X.
That orthogonality gives the normal equations X′e=0, or X′Xβ̂=X′y. When X has full column rank, solve them by multiplying by (X′X)⁻¹.

viz.caption: Projection geometry: fitted values lie in the column space of X; residuals are orthogonal to it.

ask.q: What equation expresses the residual orthogonality condition?
ask.nudge: Multiply e=y−Xβ̂ by X′ and set it equal to zero.

scenes.title: Linear model and Gauss–Markov assumptions
scenes.objective: State the assumptions before using the theorem.

blocks.body: y=Xβ+u, where y is n×1, X is a fixed or conditioned-on n×k design matrix, β is k×1 and u is the error vector.
E(u|X)=0. This makes OLS unbiased for β.
V(u|X)=σ²Iₙ. Errors have common variance and zero covariance across distinct observations.
rank(X)=k. This ensures X′X is invertible in the standard OLS formula.
The Gauss–Markov theorem does not require u to be normally distributed. Normality is used for exact finite-sample t and F distribution results in the classical model.

ask.q: Which covariance condition is stronger than merely saying every error has variance σ²?
ask.nudge: It also specifies the off-diagonal covariances.

blank.hint: Substitute V(u|X)=σ²I between A and A′.
X′X is symmetric, so its inverse is symmetric too.

steps.why: The middle product cancels one inverse factor.
This is the variance expression used in the BLUE comparison.

blocks.body: Let b=Cy be another linear estimator of β. For it to be unbiased for every β, it must satisfy CX=Iₖ.
Write C=(X′X)⁻¹X′+D. The unbiasedness condition implies DX=0.
Under V(u|X)=σ²I, Var(Cy|X)−Var(β̂|X)=σ²DD′, which is positive semidefinite.
No linear unbiased estimator has smaller variance in any linear contrast than OLS. Hence OLS is BLUE.

ask.nudge: For any vector a, consider a′DD′a.

scenes.title: Estimability: can the data identify this function?
scenes.objective: Distinguish estimating a parameter function from estimating every coefficient.
body: A design matrix may fail to identify every individual coefficient. But some combinations of coefficients can still be determined by the model's observable mean Xβ.
A linear function a′β is estimable if it can be written as a linear combination of the rows of X. Equivalently, a belongs to the column space of X′, also called the row space of X.
This is a rank-space question. It is not answered by asking whether X is square.

viz.caption: Estimability is a row-space membership question: is a in C(X′)?

scenario.title: A coefficient pair that cannot be separated
body: Suppose a regression has two identical predictor columns. The fitted mean depends on β₁+β₂, but the data cannot distinguish β₁ from β₂ individually.

The separate coefficients are not estimable because the corresponding coordinate vectors are not in the row space of X. Their sum is estimable because it is the combination the design actually measures.

A researcher can still estimate the common fitted contribution even though the individual parameter labels are not separately identifiable. The correct question is therefore whether the requested linear function lies in the row space.
This distinction prevents a common error: concluding that nothing can be estimated whenever X′X is singular.
scenario.q: If two design columns are identical, which combination is naturally identified?
scenario.answer: The sum of the two corresponding coefficients.

ask.q: What space must contain a for a′β to be estimable?
ask.nudge: Use the row space of X, equivalently the column space of X′.

scenes.title: Exam traps
scenes.objective: Separate theorem assumptions, BLUE and estimability.
scenes.intro: Mark each statement true or false and justify the decision.

items.claim: Normality of errors is required for the Gauss–Markov theorem.
items.why: The theorem uses mean and covariance assumptions, not normality.

items.claim: BLUE means minimum variance among all unbiased estimators.
items.why: The comparison class is linear unbiased estimators.

items.claim: If X has full column rank, every linear function of β is estimable.
items.why: The row space of X is all of Rᵏ.

items.claim: Equal error variances alone guarantee V(u)=σ²I.
items.why: Off-diagonal covariances must also be zero.

items.claim: If X′X is singular, no linear function of β can be estimable.
items.why: Some parameter combinations may lie in row(X) even when individual coefficients are not estimable.

scenes.title: Transfer problem: a rank-deficient design
scenes.objective: Use row-space reasoning in a design where individual coefficients are not separately estimable.
scenes.problem: Let X=[[1,1],[2,2],[3,3]]. Determine which of β₁, β₂, β₁+β₂ and β₁−β₂ are estimable.
hints: Find the row space of X; all rows are multiples of (1,1).
Test each coefficient vector a against span{(1,1)}.
A linear function is estimable exactly when its coefficient vector lies in that span.
scenes.answer: β₁ and β₂ are not separately estimable; β₁+β₂ is estimable; β₁−β₂ is not.

solution.say: The coefficient vectors for β₁ and β₂ are (1,0) and (0,1).
The coefficient vector for the sum is (1,1).
The coefficient vector for the difference is (1,−1).

ask.q: What is the key difference between β₁+β₂ and β₁−β₂ here?
ask.nudge: One coefficient vector follows the only direction present in the rows of X.

scenes.title: Summary: the theorem and the exam workflow
scenes.objective: Recall the Gauss–Markov and estimability decision procedures.
body: Start with y=Xβ+u. Under E(u|X)=0, V(u|X)=σ²I and full column rank, OLS is β̂=(X′X)⁻¹X′y, is unbiased and has variance σ²(X′X)⁻¹. The Gauss–Markov theorem makes it BLUE among linear unbiased estimators. Normality is not required.
For a′β, test whether a lies in row(X), equivalently C(X′). Full column rank makes every linear function estimable; rank deficiency may leave some combinations estimable and others not.
For the June 2026 anchor, construct X carefully. The cross-product matrix is diag(6,2), so the correct divisors are 6 for β̂₁ and 2 for β̂₂. Verify the result by multiplying back.

ask.q: State the two central conclusions of this lesson.
ask.nudge: One concerns optimality among linear unbiased estimators; the other concerns row-space membership.

scenes.title: Extension — the proof with Q11's numbers
scenes.objective: See the variance split a′a + d′d numerically.

blocks.body: For Q11, X′ is 2×3, so its null space is one-dimensional. The vector z = (1, −1, 1)/√3 satisfies X′z = 0: its first entry gives (1 − 2 + 1)/√3 = 0 and its second gives (1 − 1)/√3 = 0.
Any linear unbiased estimator of β₁ has weights c = (1,2,1)/6 + tz. Its variance is σ²c′c = σ²(1/6 + t²), because the OLS weights are orthogonal to z.
At t = 0 the variance is σ²/6, the smallest. At t = 1 it is 7σ²/6, at t = 2 it is 25σ²/6. Every competitor is OLS plus a term that adds variance and nothing else.

ask.q: Why is the cross term 2a′d zero?
ask.nudge: d is built to satisfy d′X = 0.
